subject: botany_2
question_text: What are some bio-safety issues concerned with genetically modified crops?

mark_split.label: Risk to human and animal health

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.35, printed question 46. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

insider_note: Five issues in the book. The one an examiner most wants is GENE POLLUTION leading to super weeds — write it even if the others are brief.

steps.label: Risk to human and animal health
steps.margin_note: Name both allergens and toxins, and say the effect may be long term.
lines: 1. ALLERGIES AND TOXINS:
There is a fear that a transferred gene may
produce a protein that acts as an ALLERGEN or a
TOXIN in humans and animals.
The effect may appear only as a long term side
effect, after years of consumption.
steps.why: A gene moved into a food crop makes a protein people have never eaten before, and its effects can only be established over time.
common_mistakes: Saying GM crops are known to be toxic. The issue is a RISK, not a proven harm.
Leaving out allergies. Allergenicity is the first named concern.
steps.memory_tip: A new protein in an old food is the first worry.

steps.label: Risk to food and biodiversity
steps.margin_note: Both issues numbered, with one concrete mechanism.
lines: 2. CHANGE TO THE FOOD ITSELF:
There is a risk of changing the fundamental
nature of vegetables and other foods.
3. HARM TO BIODIVERSITY:
GM crops may harm biodiversity and have an
adverse impact on the environment, for example
by killing non-target insects.
steps.why: A toxin meant for one pest is present in every cell of the plant, so insects that were never the target meet it too.
common_mistakes: Saying GM crops affect only the target pest. Non-target insects may be affected too.
Giving one issue where the question asks for several.
steps.memory_tip: A toxin in every cell meets more than the pest it was meant for.

steps.label: Risk to evolution
steps.margin_note: The general issue plus the resistance mechanism.
lines: 4. CHANGES TO EVOLUTIONARY PATTERNS:
GM crops may bring about changes in natural
evolutionary patterns.
Pests exposed continuously to one toxin may
evolve RESISTANCE to it, so the crop stops
working.
steps.why: Constant exposure to a single toxin is the strongest possible selection pressure, so resistant pests are the expected outcome rather than a surprise.
common_mistakes: Saying evolution is not affected. Continuous selection pressure is exactly what drives resistance.
Giving no mechanism. Resistance evolving in the pest is the concrete case.
steps.memory_tip: A toxin used everywhere selects for pests that survive it.

steps.label: Gene pollution and super weeds
steps.margin_note: Name gene pollution, the mechanism, the consequence, and GEAC. This is the strongest mark.

lines.text: Transgenes escaping into wild relatives can

lines: 5. GENE POLLUTION:
New genes may be transferred into related WILD
species by natural out-crossing.
This can produce SUPER WEEDS, which grow faster
than the crop and are resistant to weedicides.
This is why the GEAC must approve any GM release.
steps.why: Pollen does not respect field boundaries, so a herbicide-tolerance gene can move into the very weeds the herbicide was meant to kill.
common_mistakes: Leaving out super weeds. It is the named consequence and the most memorable issue.
Saying gene pollution means chemical pollution. It means GENES escaping into wild relatives.
steps.memory_tip: The escaped gene ends up in the weed.
